label: Algebra-Geometry Dictionary
notes: This chapter covers printed pages 177 through 236 and makes the correspondence between ideals and varieties precise. Over an algebraically closed field the Nullstellensatz translates geometric statements about varieties into algebraic statements about ideals, giving a genuine dictionary in which radical ideals match varieties exactly.

label: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
notes: The weak Nullstellensatz says a system of polynomials has no common solution over an algebraically closed field exactly when the constant one lies in their ideal. The strong form identifies the polynomials vanishing on a variety as the radical of the defining ideal, the cornerstone of the entire dictionary.

label: Radical Ideals
notes: The radical of an ideal collects every polynomial some power of which lies in the ideal. The Nullstellensatz gives an inclusion-reversing bijection between affine varieties and radical ideals, so passing to the radical loses no geometric information while making the algebra and geometry correspond perfectly.

label: Sums, Products, Intersections
notes: Set-theoretic operations on varieties correspond to ideal operations: unions match intersections of ideals, intersections match sums, and products of ideals also cut out unions. These dictionary entries let us compute geometric constructions purely algebraically using Grobner basis techniques for each operation.

label: Zariski Closure and Quotients
notes: The Zariski closure of a set is the smallest variety containing it, computed as the variety of the ideal of all vanishing polynomials. The ideal quotient, or colon ideal, corresponds to closure of a set difference, allowing us to remove unwanted components from a variety algebraically.

label: Irreducible Varieties
notes: A variety is irreducible exactly when its ideal is prime, and every variety decomposes uniquely into finitely many irreducible components matching the minimal primes of its radical. This decomposition organizes the geometry and sets up the coordinate ring study. Next: functions on a variety.
